```{r}
#Part A
m1 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
print(m1)
m2 <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
print(m2)
scores <- matrix(c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84, 90), nrow = 2, ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE)
rownames(scores) <- c("Quiz1", "Quiz2")
colnames(scores) <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid")

print(scores)

#Question 1
#R fills a matrix column by column, it takes the first value and places it in row 1 column 1, then moves down before moving right. Adding byrow = TRUE changes the fill direction to row by row

#Question 2
matrix(1:8, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
#R recycles the input vector to fill the missing 9th slot, it loops back to the beginning of 1:8 and reuses 1 to fill the last cell.

#Part B
print(scores[1, 2])
print(scores[1, ])
print(scores[, "Ben"])

print(scores[scores >= 90])

#Question 3
class(scores[1, ])
class(scores[, "Ben"])
#Both return "integer". 

#Question 4
#scores[1, ] uses positional indexing. This tells R exactly which row to extract while keeping the column dimension intact.

#Part C
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2)
b <- matrix(5:8, nrow = 2)

print(dim(scores))
print(nrow(scores))
print(ncol(scores))

scores_t <- t(scores)
print(scores_t)
print(dim(scores_t))

print(a + b)
print(a * b)

print(a %*% b)

#Question 5
#(a * b) pairs each cell in a with the cell at the exact same position in b and multiplies them directly. Matrix multiplication (a %*% b), each cell in the result is computed by taking an entire row from a and an entire column from b, multiplying their corresponding elements, and sums together.

#Question 6
#In the original scores, the row represents (Quiz1, Quiz2) and the column(Ana, Ben, Cid). When transposed, rows become columns and columns become rows.

#Part D
scores_v2 <- cbind(scores, Dex = c(85, 91))
print(scores_v2)

scores_v3 <- rbind(scores, Quiz3 = c(80, 88, 93))
print(scores_v3)

#Question 7
cbind(scores, c(85, 91, 100))
#scores has 2 rows, but the vector provided has 3 values. There is no valid way to align them column-wise because each row in the existing matrix needs exactly one corresponding value in the new column.

#Question 8
#rbind() when new observations are added over time while the variables stay the same. 

#Part E
arr <- array(1:12, dim = c(2, 3, 2))
print(arr)

print(arr[1, 2, 2])
print(arr[, , 1])

print(dim(arr))

#Question 9
#dim(arr) returns c(2, 3, 2), and each number maps to one index in arr[row, col, layer]. 

#Question 10
#A natural real-world fit for a 3D array is monthly sales data across multiple stores and products. Rows represent products, columns represent stores, and each layer represents a different month. January’s sales sit in layer 1, February’s in layer 2, and so on. A single 2D matrix would not be enough because it can only hold one snapshot at a time.

#Part F
class_a <- matrix(c(85, 90, 78, 92), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S1", "S2"), c("Midterm", "Final")))
class_b <- matrix(c(88, 84, 95, 91), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE,
                  dimnames = list(c("S3", "S4"), c("Midterm", "Final")))

all_students <- rbind(class_a, class_b)
print(all_students)

print(rowMeans(all_students))
```
